subject: Pathology
summary: A full blood count (FBC) gives a snapshot of red cells, white cells and platelets, helping detect anaemia, infection, inflammation or bone‑marrow disease. It guides diagnosis, monitoring and treatment decisions.

sections.p: An FBC measures haemoglobin, red cell indices, white cell differential, and platelet count, usually via automated haematology analyser.
b: Haemoglobin (Hb)
Hematocrit (Hct)
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH)
White cell count (WCC)
Differential (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes)
Platelet count

sections.p: Interpretation uses reference ranges and clinical context. For anaemia, WHO grades severity by Hb thresholds; for infection, WCC and differential patterns suggest bacterial vs viral.
b: Anaemia: Hb <13 g/dL (men), <12 g/dL (women); severe <7 g/dL

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, infections dominate, followed by nutritional deficiencies and hemoglobinopathies.
b: Malignancy: leukaemia, lymphoma

sections.p: FBC abnormalities appear as laboratory findings; clinical clues include fatigue, pallor, fever, bruising or bleeding.
b: Thrombocytopenia: petechiae, easy bruising

sections.p: The FBC is the first test; further workup depends on abnormal results.

faq.q: What is the normal range for haemoglobin?
faq.a: ~13.5–17.5 g/dL in men, 12–15.5 g/dL in women.

faq.q: Why is a high eosinophil count important?
faq.a: It suggests parasitic infection, allergic disease or hypereosinophilic syndrome.

faq.q: Can an FBC be normal in infection?
faq.a: Yes, early infection may show normal counts; repeat testing or other markers (CRP, procalcitonin) help.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Her FBC shows Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 10 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis and first step in management?
A 45‑year‑old man with fever has WCC 18 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 85%, platelets 80 × 10⁹/L. What red flag should prompt urgent referral?
A child in a malaria‑endemic area has Hb 8 g/dL, MCV 80 fL, and a positive malaria smear. What is the appropriate treatment strategy?

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam allow you to interpret the FBC in context and to identify red‑flag features that need urgent action.
b: Onset, duration and progression of fatigue, dyspnoea or bruising
Dietary intake, especially iron, folate and vitamin B12 sources
Recent infections, malaria, helminthic exposure, HIV or TB symptoms
Medication and herbal use that can cause marrow suppression or haemolysis
Menstrual history, obstetric history and contraceptive use
Family history of haemoglobinopathies or haematological malignancy
Occupational or environmental exposures (benzene, radiation)

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or hepatomegaly; presence suggests anaemia, haemolysis or infiltrative disease
Percuss liver edge, then palpate for firm or enlarged spleen; a palpable spleen >2 cm below costal margin indicates splenomegaly, common in haemolysis or myeloproliferative disorders
Palpate cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal nodes; firm, non‑tender nodes raise suspicion of lymphoma or leukaemia
Identify petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses or oral ulceration; positive findings suggest thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction
Detect a flow murmur in severe anaemia; a new systolic murmur may indicate high‑output state
Check for peripheral neuropathy (B12 deficiency) or focal deficits (leukaemic infiltration); bedside test cannot quantify nerve damage

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Interpretation of the automated full blood count requires calculated indices and correlation with clinical context; when a test is unavailable, use surrogate clinical markers.
b: Hb: <13 g/dL men, <12 g/dL women defines anaemia; <7 g/dL is severe and usually warrants transfusion
Hct roughly 3 × Hb; low Hct confirms anaemia severity
MCV: <80 fL microcytic, 80‑100 fL normocytic, >100 fL macrocytic; guides iron vs. B12/folate work‑up
MCHC: low in iron deficiency, normal in thalassaemia trait
RDW: >14 % suggests mixed population, common in iron deficiency or early B12 deficiency

t.b: Low ferritin (<30 ng/mL) confirms iron deficiency; if unavailable, use transferrin saturation <20 % and peripheral smear microcytosis
Level <150 pmol/L indicates deficiency; if unavailable, check methylmalonic acid or homocysteine elevation
Serum folate <3 ng/mL suggests deficiency; red cell folate is preferred when possible
Absolute retic >100 ×10⁹/L or retic index >2 indicates appropriate marrow response (haemolysis or blood loss); low retic points to production problem
Morphology (microcytosis, macro‑ovalocytes, blasts, schistocytes) refines differential; presence of >10 % blasts suggests acute leukaemia
High LDH with low haptoglobin supports haemolysis; normal haptoglobin does not exclude intravascular haemolysis if sample delayed
Positive direct Coombs confirms immune‑mediated haemolysis; negative result shifts focus to mechanical or hereditary causes
Required when blasts >10 % in peripheral blood, unexplained pancytopenia, or suspicion of myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative disease; provides definitive classification

sections.p: Classification integrates quantitative thresholds with morphological and clinical data to guide management and prognosis.
b: Anaemia severity by WHO: mild (Hb 11‑12 g/dL women, 11‑13 g/dL men), moderate (Hb 8‑10 g/dL), severe (Hb <8 g/dL)
Microcytic anaemia with ferritin <30 ng/mL → iron‑deficiency anaemia; treat with oral iron, monitor Hb rise 1 g/dL/2 weeks
Macrocytic anaemia with B12 <150 pmol/L or folate <3 ng/mL → treat with parenteral B12 or folate, assess for malabsorption

t.b: Uses morphology, immunophenotype, genetics; CML defined by BCR‑ABL1 fusion, chronic phase WCC 100‑500 ×10⁹/L, basophilia >2 % and splenomegaly

t.a: International Prognostic Scoring System for MDS
t.b: Scores based on cytopenias, blast percentage, cytogenetics; low‑risk (IPSS ≤0.5) managed conservatively, high‑risk (>1.5) considered for disease‑modifying therapy
Del(17p) or TP53 mutation places patient in high‑risk group, influencing choice of targeted therapy

sections.p: Several non‑haematological disorders can mimic FBC abnormalities; careful correlation with history, exam and targeted tests separates them.
b: Iron deficiency vs. thalassaemia trait: both microcytic; iron studies (low ferritin) differentiate, RBC count higher in thalassaemia

t.b: Normocytic or mildly microcytic, ferritin normal/high, low iron, low TIBC; history of infection, TB, rheumatoid disease points to this

t.a: Hemolytic anemia vs. acute blood loss
t.b: Both cause low Hb; retic count high in hemolysis, low in acute loss; LDH high and haptoglobin low favour haemolysis

t.a: Reactive neutrophilia vs. chronic myeloid leukaemia
t.b: Reactive: left shift with toxic granulation, normal basophils; CML: marked basophilia, very high WCC, presence of myelocytes and metamyelocytes, BCR‑ABL1 positive

sections.p: A systematic approach to abnormal FBC results ensures rapid stabilization, correct aetiology treatment and safe monitoring, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Verify sample integrity and repeat if haemolysis or clotted sample suspected.
2. Stabilise the patient: give oxygen, IV fluids, treat fever, and correct severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL) or thrombocytopenia (<10 ×10⁹/L) with transfusion.

3. Identify the dominant cytopenia (anaemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and order targeted confirmatory tests (iron studies, peripheral smear, malaria smear, HIV test, bone‑marrow aspirate).

4. Initiate disease‑specific therapy: antimalarials for malaria‑related anaemia, iron/folate for nutritional deficits, antibiotics for bacterial sepsis, disease‑modifying agents for leukaemia (hydroxyurea, tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors).
5. Monitor trends: repeat full blood count every 24‑48 h in acute settings, weekly in chronic disease, and after each therapeutic intervention.
6. Escalate or refer if: haemodynamic instability, Hb <7 g/dL despite transfusion, WCC >100 ×10⁹/L with blasts, platelets <20 ×10⁹/L with active bleeding, or diagnostic uncertainty.
7. Document response and plan long‑term follow‑up: iron repletion, malaria prophylaxis, chronic disease monitoring, or oncology referral.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Common drugs used for FBC abnormalities have predictable adverse profiles; recognising them prevents iatrogenic harm.
b: Iron salts – cause gastrointestinal irritation and constipation; give with vitamin C, avoid with antacids.
Folic acid – generally safe; high doses may mask B12 deficiency, so check B12 if neuropathy appears.
Hydroxyurea – myelosuppression and renal toxicity; monitor CBC weekly, hold if neutrophils <1 ×10⁹/L.
Tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors (e.g., imatinib) – cause cytopenias and hepatic enzyme rise; check LFTs monthly, avoid in severe liver failure.
G‑CSF – bone pain and rare splenic rupture; pause if severe bone pain or splenomegaly worsens.
Tranexamic acid – reduces bleeding but may increase thrombosis risk; avoid in active thromboembolic disease.

sections.p: Cytopenias can precipitate life‑threatening events; early recognition of complications triggers timely escalation.
b: Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL) → cardiac strain, syncope; give packed red cells and consider ICU transfer.
Neutropenia (ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L) → bacterial sepsis; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, add antifungal if fever persists >5 days.
Thrombocytopenia (<20 ×10⁹/L) with mucosal bleeding → platelet transfusion and investigate for DIC.
Leukocytosis with >20 % blasts → acute leukaemia; urgent bone‑marrow biopsy and oncology referral.
Eosinophilia >1.5 ×10⁹/L with organ dysfunction → hypereosinophilic syndrome; start high‑dose steroids and refer to haematology.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and external influences modify both the laboratory picture and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV – can cause anaemia of chronic disease, neutropenia from drugs, and opportunistic infections that raise WCC; CD4 count guides prophylaxis.
TB – often presents with normocytic anaemia and mild leukocytosis; rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, reducing efficacy of some antileukaemic drugs.
Malnutrition – low ferritin (<30 ng/mL) indicates iron deficiency; vitamin B12 deficiency gives macrocytosis, so check B12 before giving folate alone.
Pregnancy – plasma volume expands, lowering Hb; use pregnancy‑adjusted reference ranges and avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., methotrexate).
Diabetes – chronic kidney disease can cause anaemia of renal disease; erythropoietin may be required if Hb <10 g/dL.
Herbal remedies (e.g., papaya leaf extract) – may cause thrombocytopenia; obtain a full medication history.
Alcohol excess – macrocytosis, folate deficiency, and liver‑related thrombocytopenia; counsel cessation.
Renal failure – reduces erythropoietin, alters drug clearance; dose‑adjust G‑CSF and avoid nephrotoxic agents.

sections.p: Tailoring assessment and treatment to vulnerable populations improves outcomes where resources are limited.
b: Children – use age‑specific reference ranges; consider malaria, sickle cell disease, and nutritional anaemia; avoid adult‑dose iron tablets.
Pregnancy – prioritize maternal haemoglobin >11 g/dL; give oral iron, folic acid, and treat malaria promptly; defer teratogenic chemotherapy until postpartum.
Elderly – higher cardiovascular risk with anaemia; maintain Hb ≥10 g/dL; avoid aggressive transfusion thresholds and monitor for drug interactions.
People with HIV – screen for opportunistic infections, adjust doses for protease‑inhibitor interactions, and use prophylactic antibiotics when CD4 <200 cells/µL.

Low‑resource settings – rely on peripheral smear, malaria rapid test, and clinical scoring when automated counters unavailable; use oral iron and folate, and refer only when life‑threatening cytopenias develop.

vivas.q: What are the three key history questions when a patient presents with unexplained anaemia?
vivas.a: Onset and duration of symptoms, dietary intake and menstrual/bleeding history, and exposure to infections or chronic disease.

vivas.q: How do you perform and interpret a peripheral smear for reactive neutrophilia versus leukaemia?
vivas.a: Look for left‑shift with toxic granules, Dӧhle bodies and normal maturation; leukaemia shows blasts, abnormal nuclei, and dysplasia.

vivas.q: Why must the FBC tube contain K₂EDTA and not heparin?
vivas.a: EDTA chelates calcium preventing clotting while preserving cell morphology; heparin can cause platelet clumping and inaccurate counts.

vivas.q: What bedside sign helps differentiate true thrombocytopenia from platelet clumping?
vivas.a: A smear showing platelet aggregates suggests pseudothrombocytopenia; repeat with citrate tube if needed.

vivas.q: When is a bone‑marrow aspirate mandatory in a patient with WCC 40 ×10⁹/L and 25 % blasts?
vivas.a: Any blast percentage ≥10 % with cytopenias or high WCC warrants marrow to confirm acute leukaemia.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a low MCV with normal ferritin in a malaria‑endemic child.
vivas.a: Suggests thalassaemia trait; iron studies are normal, and red cell indices guide further testing.

vivas.q: What is the first step after finding isolated lymphocytosis with smudge cells?
vivas.a: Consider chronic lymphocytic leukaemia; order immunophenotyping (CD5, CD19, CD23) for confirmation.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection alter the interpretation of a full blood count?
vivas.a: May cause anaemia of chronic disease, neutropenia, lymphocytosis, or thrombocytopenia; CD4 count guides urgency of work‑up.

vivas.q: What is the management hierarchy for severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL) in a pregnant woman?
vivas.a: Stabilise haemodynamically, give cross‑matched packed RBCs, treat underlying cause, monitor fetal status.

vivas.q: Why is it important to repeat the FBC after 24 hours in suspected drug‑induced neutropenia?
vivas.a: To confirm a falling neutrophil trend and decide on G‑CSF use; transient drops may resolve spontaneously.

vivas.q: What are the red‑flag laboratory features of sepsis on an FBC?
vivas.a: Leukocytosis >15 ×10⁹/L, neutrophilia >80 %, left shift, and thrombocytopenia <150 ×10⁹/L suggest severe infection.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate iron‑deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease using ferritin and CRP?
vivas.a: Ferritin <30 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency; normal/high ferritin with elevated CRP points to chronic disease.

vivas.q: What is the appropriate transfusion trigger for a patient with active gastrointestinal bleeding?
vivas.a: Platelet count <50 ×10⁹/L and Hb <8 g/dL; give platelets and packed cells respectively.

vivas.q: When should growth‑factor therapy be considered in chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia?
vivas.a: If ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L and febrile or high‑risk regimen; not for routine pancytopenia without infection risk.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot reliably assess platelet function?
vivas.a: Platelet count; it does not measure aggregation or adhesion, which require bleeding time or platelet function analyser.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with fever has WCC 18 ×10⁹/L, neutrophils 85 %, platelets 80 ×10⁹/L. Which finding most strongly suggests a life‑threatening complication?
mcqs.e: Neutrophilia with thrombocytopenia signals consumptive sepsis or DIC.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the correct prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold in a stable adult?
mcqs.e: Guidelines recommend transfusion when platelets are <10 ×10⁹/L in stable patients.

mcqs.q: A child in a malaria‑endemic area has Hb 8 g/dL, MCV 80 fL, positive malaria smear. Which additional test best distinguishes iron‑deficiency from thalassaemia trait?
mcqs.e: Low ferritin (<30 ng/mL) confirms iron deficiency; thalassaemia has normal ferritin.

mcqs.q: Which peripheral blood film pattern confirms reactive neutrophilia?
o: Toxic granulation, Dӧhle bodies, left shift
mcqs.e: Toxic granules and Dӧhle bodies indicate a reactive process.

mcqs.q: In a patient with isolated lymphocytosis and smudge cells, the next best test is:
A 62‑year‑old with fatigue, fever, bruising has WCC 40 ×10⁹/L, 25 % blasts. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Bone‑marrow aspirate with flow cytometry is definitive for acute leukaemia.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and menorrhagia. FBC: Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, WCC 6 ×10⁹/L, platelets 210 ×10⁹/L. Ferritin 25 ng/mL.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Iron‑deficiency anaemia due to chronic blood loss.

qs.q: Which single laboratory parameter confirms iron deficiency?
What is the first management step?
qs.a: Start oral iron supplementation and address menstrual bleeding.

cases.v: A 55‑year‑old man with weight loss, splenomegaly, and leukocytosis (WCC 140 ×10⁹/L) shows neutrophilia, left shift, and basophilia. No blasts on smear.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: BCR‑ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome) detection by PCR or FISH.

qs.q: Initial treatment in a low‑resource setting?
qs.a: Start a tyrosine‑kinase inhibitor (e.g., imatinib) if available; otherwise refer for specialist care.

mistakes: Using ferritin <15 ng/mL as the iron‑deficiency cut‑off, missing many cases.
Transfusing platelets prophylactically at <30 ×10⁹/L instead of the recommended <10 ×10⁹/L in stable patients.
Giving G‑CSF for any pancytopenia without neutropenia or infection risk.
Confusing reactive eosinophilia (>1.5 ×10⁹/L) with hypereosinophilic syndrome without clinical organ involvement.
